extracted.intended_audience: students and educated readers of political history and public policy
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative principles for how the United States (and similar powers) should acquire, organize, govern, and judge transmarine dominions, and for understanding American political doctrines (e.g., laissez-faire) that shape such policy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Different acquisitions require distinct modes of administration
rubrics_metrics.description: Each acquisition may be dealt with in a separate and distinct way (example: Hawaii erected into a Territory with governor and legislature; Puerto Rico given a colonial organization with a partly-elected lower house and an appointed upper house; Guam and Tutuila treated as naval coaling stations; the Philippines administered with municipal councils and native appointments).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose administrative form to suit local conditions (population makeup, existing institutions, strategic purposes). Examples show a spectrum from full territorial organization to colonial administration to military/coaling-station control.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criteria for admitting a territory as a State
rubrics_metrics.description: Admission prospects depend on demographic composition (stock of American/British settlers vs non‑European populations), language, and political/cultural fit with constitutional self-government.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hawaii: small American/British population and large immigrant/native groups make statehood unlikely despite Constitution being in force; evaluate likelihood of successful constitutional self-government before statehood.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sufficiency of local political institutions (Puerto Rico model)
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate legislative structure, suffrage limits, appointment of officials, and degree of autonomy offered to inhabitants when judging the adequacy of governance arrangements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Puerto Rico example: lower house elected on limited suffrage, upper house largely appointed — inhabitants may desire fuller autonomy; language and literacy levels (Spanish-only, low literacy) affect readiness and shape what arrangements are practical.

rubrics_metrics.name: Administrative fitness and readiness for self-government (Philippines)
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess population civility, level of political development, and capacity for local administration when deciding retention, annexation, or preparation for self-government.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Indicators of progress include establishment of municipal councils elected by the people, appointment of natives to administrative posts, public works (roads), sanitary reforms, education enrollment, and settlement of former power-holders (e.g., friars) on liberal terms. Continued local disturbances or guerrilla warfare are negative indicators; restrictions (e.g., banning Chinese immigration, limiting corporate land ownership) are policy responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sanitary measures as a test and duty of administration
rubrics_metrics.description: A government (or occupying power) should carry out sanitary measures to prevent epidemic and infectious diseases; success in this is both a moral and practical mark of competent rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Canal Zone and Cuba examples: removal of yellow fever and malaria through sanitary work is cited as an admirable service; the Platt Amendment required Cuba to carry out sanitary measures as a condition of relations with the U.S.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal and constitutional fit for applying domestic constitution to distant possessions
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize difficulty in adjusting a constitution framed for a domestic polity to remote countries inhabited by alien peoples and held by force; the legal status of inhabitants and the applicability of constitutional protections may be unclear.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Canal Zone administration by War Department left inhabitants' status under the Federal Constitution not precisely determined; expect legal complexity when extending domestic law overseas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of naval and military strength balanced by restraint
rubrics_metrics.description: While overwhelming naval strength makes defense or enforcement easier, wise statesmen should resist temptation to permanent intervention, annexation, or ruling foreign peoples unless clearly justified.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical lesson: interventions that seem justifiable can lead unintentionally to annexation (examples: British India, Russian Central Asia). Prefer restraint, avoid aggressive or overbearing actions that would rekindle regional suspicions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intervention permitted to preserve independence and adequate government (Platt-style conditions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Intervention may be justified when necessary for preservation of a country's independence and maintenance of a government adequate to protect life, property, and individual liberty; the weaker state may accept limitations (e.g., leases for naval stations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Platt Amendment clauses required Cuba not to permit foreign powers to obtain lodgment, allowed U.S. intervention to preserve Cuban independence and adequate government, required sanitary measures, and allowed leases of land for coaling/naval stations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economic instruments and investment as measures of bilateral relations
rubrics_metrics.description: Reciprocal tariff arrangements and flow of capital are indicators of closeness in relations and are tools for shaping ties between states and territories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: reciprocal tariff reductions between U.S. and Cuba and heavy American capital investment underline closer commercial ties without formal annexation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fitness for self-government judged by language, race, and literacy
rubrics_metrics.description: Readiness for self-government is assessed by whether inhabitants speak the ruling/constitutional language, the racial composition relative to existing polity, and educational attainment (literacy rates).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Puerto Rico cited: Spanish-only language, significant 'negro element', and only 17% literacy among certain groups argued for delaying fuller autonomy or statehood until qualifications improve.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid further annexations absent clear benefits
rubrics_metrics.description: Policy should aim to avoid further conquests or annexations, particularly of tropical territories with populations dissimilar to the annexing country, unless clear political and social fit exists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argument: new tropical territories may have populations not of American or North European stock and would either be governed as colonies or admitted as states, both options posing grave difficulties for American democratic political life; contemporary administrations generally opposed further annexations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Democratic government requires equality and homogeneity of citizens
rubrics_metrics.description: Successful democratic self-government is argued to require a level of equality and homogeneity among citizens; large disparities in language, political habit, or race may impede democratic functioning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author's view: transplantation of Declaration-style institutions to tropical lands with backward races is problematic; admitting culturally and linguistically different populations as states may be detrimental.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer arbitration and pacific instruments over war or annexation
rubrics_metrics.description: States should favor arbitration, treaty mechanisms, and international institutions to settle disputes and avoid war or heavy-handed interventions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: arbitration treaties with Canada, urging courts of arbitration for Central America, setting up a Central American Court of Arbitration in conjunction with Mexico are presented as positive measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primacy of certain individual rights (American dogma)
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain individual rights — e.g., the right to enjoy what one has earned and the right to free expression — are primordial and sacred.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This dogma underpins an American political outlook that privileges individual liberty and property, informing resistance to broad governmental interference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Political power springs from the people; popular government preferred
rubrics_metrics.description: All political power is asserted to spring from the people, and the most completely popular government is judged to be the best form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This principle legitimizes democratic rule and majoritarian decision-making in American political thought as recounted by the author.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strict legal limits on legislatures and officials
rubrics_metrics.description: Legislatures, officials, and agents of the sovereign people ought to be strictly limited by law, by mutual checks, and by short terms of office.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Short terms and legal limits are intended to keep officials accountable and to prevent accumulation of power; this is presented as a core American maxims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preference for decentralization: local over central authority
rubrics_metrics.description: Where any function can be equally well discharged by a central or a local body, it ought by preference to be entrusted to the local body to avoid tyranny, inefficiency, and corruption.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argument: small-scale local administration is closer to citizen knowledge and more sensitive to opinion; centralization is more likely to be tyrannical and impure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Majority rule as the basis of political legitimacy
rubrics_metrics.description: The will of the larger number must prevail against the smaller; the majority's authority rests on numerical superiority rather than special moral standing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Nation is conceived as the sum of individuals; majority rule is justified pragmatically rather than metaphysically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Laissez-faire principle: minimize government functions
rubrics_metrics.description: The less government the better — governmental functions should be kept at a minimum to maximize individual and community prosperity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two foundations: sentimental (desire to be let alone) and rational (belief that state interference often harms more than it helps). The author notes historical roots in Anglo-American traditions and questions the practical limits of the 'minimum' in changing modern conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rational foundation for non-interference: natural social laws and spontaneous order
rubrics_metrics.description: Non-interference is defended on the rational ground that the natural collision and cooperation of individual impulses tend to produce better social outcomes than conscious state direction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This view is contrasted with continental European theories that stress state action; in America it commonly appears as a pragmatic faith in individual enterprise as the engine of national success.
